section.title: Wealth, Poverty, and Instruction
section.sectionRationale: Continuing the first Solomonic collection, 10:1 to 22:16, this chapter clusters proverbs on integrity versus riches gained by folly, the fragile loyalty that money buys, the discipline of children, and the LORD's purpose standing firm over every human plan.
section.thesis: Integrity outweighs riches, kindness to the poor is a loan to the LORD Himself, and though many plans fill a man's heart, it is the purpose of the LORD that stands, so wisdom means accepting instruction and fearing Him rather than chasing wealth or resenting discipline.
section.frameNote: Six clusters: integrity better than riches or haste; friendship, false witness, and the favor money buys; the LORD's purpose stands; discipline your son while there is hope; the fear of the LORD leads to life; final warnings against sloth, cruelty, and rebellion.

units.label: Integrity better than riches or haste
units.note: the poor who walk with integrity

verses.text: Better a poor man who walks with integrity than a fool whose lips are perverse.
Even zeal is no good without knowledge, and he who hurries his footsteps misses the mark.
A man's own folly subverts his way, yet his heart rages against the LORD.

units.label: Friendship, false witness, and the favor money buys

verses.text: Wealth attracts many friends, but a poor man is deserted by his friend.
A false witness will not go unpunished, and one who utters lies will not escape.
Many seek the favor of the prince, and everyone is a friend of the gift giver.
All the brothers of a poor man hate him, how much more do his friends avoid him! He may pursue them with pleading, but they are nowhere to be found.
He who acquires {{chokmah|wisdom}} loves himself; one who safeguards understanding will find success.
A false witness will not go unpunished, and one who pours out lies will perish.
Luxury is unseemly for a fool, how much worse for a slave to rule over princes!

units.label: The LORD's purpose stands
units.note: patience, kingship, and the fear of the LORD

verses.text: A man's insight gives him patience, and his virtue is to overlook an offense.
A king's rage is like the roar of a lion, but his favor is like dew on the grass.
A foolish son is his father's ruin, and a quarrelsome wife is like a constant dripping.
Houses and wealth are inherited from fathers, but a prudent wife is from the LORD.
Laziness brings on deep sleep, and an idle soul will suffer hunger.
He who keeps a commandment preserves his soul, but he who is careless in his ways will die.
Kindness to the poor is a loan to the LORD, and He will repay the lender.

units.label: Discipline your son while there is hope

verses.text: Discipline your son, for in that there is hope; do not be party to his death.
A man of great anger must pay the penalty; if you rescue him, you will have to do so again.
Listen to counsel and accept discipline, that you may be wise the rest of your days.

units.label: The fear of the LORD leads to life
units.note: the LORD's purpose over man's plans

verses.text: Many plans are in a man's heart, but the purpose of the LORD will prevail.
The desire of a man is loving devotion; better to be poor than a liar.
The {{yirah|fear}} of the LORD leads to life, that one may rest content, without visitation from harm.
The slacker buries his hand in the dish; he will not even bring it back to his mouth.
Strike a mocker, and the simple will beware; rebuke the discerning man, and he will gain knowledge.
He who assaults his father or evicts his mother is a son who brings shame and disgrace.
If you cease to hear instruction, my son, you will stray from the words of knowledge.
A corrupt witness mocks justice, and a wicked mouth swallows iniquity.
Judgments are prepared for mockers, and beatings for the backs of fools.

chokmah.gloss: Wisdom, the skill of living rightly before God and others. Verse 8 says whoever acquires it 'loves himself,' meaning true self-love is not indulgence but the pursuit of wisdom, since wisdom preserves the very soul that pursues it.

yirah.gloss: Fear, reverent awe. Verse 23 says this fear of the LORD leads to life and lets a person rest content, untouched by real harm, the same fear that Proverbs 1:7 calls the beginning of knowledge.

basic.context: This chapter weighs integrity against wealth gained by folly or flattery, exposes how money buys fickle friendship while poverty drives even family away, and calls fathers to discipline their sons while there is hope. It closes with the great truth that though people make many plans, it is the LORD's purpose that finally prevails.
basic.hermeneutics: These proverbs describe patterns of life, not ironclad guarantees; not every poor person has integrity and not every rich person lacks it, but the chapter consistently ranks character above cash and warns that wealth's friendships are often fickle while the LORD's favor toward the faithful is not.
basic.originalLanguages: Chokmah, wisdom, verse 8, is something a person acquires for the sake of his own soul, since pursuing it is true self-love, not selfishness. Yirah, the fear of the LORD, verse 23, leads to life and rest, echoing the refrain of Proverbs that reverence for God, not self-reliance, is the beginning of true living.
basic.typology: Kindness to the poor as a loan to the LORD, verse 17, anticipates Christ's identification with the poor and needy, Matthew 25:40, where kindness shown to the least is kindness shown to Him. The father's discipline of a son while there is hope, verse 18, foreshadows the discipline of the Father who disciplines those He loves, Hebrews 12:6.
basic.christ: Verse 17 says kindness to the poor is a loan to the LORD, who will repay the lender, a truth Christ makes explicit when He says whatever is done for the least of His brothers is done for Him, Matthew 25:40. And the chapter's confidence that the LORD's purpose will prevail over every human plan, verse 21, is the same confidence the gospel rests on, that God's redemptive plan in Christ cannot be overturned by human scheming, Acts 4:27 to 28.
basic.god: God is the true creditor behind every act of mercy to the poor, verse 17, and the sovereign whose purpose stands firm no matter how many plans fill the human heart, verse 21. He disciplines those He loves the way a wise father disciplines a son while there is hope, verse 18, aiming always at life, not despair.
basic.crossReferences: Matthew 25:34-40 shows Christ identifying with the poor, fulfilling the loan to the LORD of 19:17. Hebrews 12:5-11 develops fatherly discipline for our good. Acts 4:27-28 shows the LORD's purpose prevailing even through human plots. James 1:19-20 echoes the patience and slowness to anger commended in 19:11.
basic.oneStory: Proverbs 19 calls God's people to integrity over wealth, mercy to the poor, patient discipline of children, and trust that the LORD's purpose will prevail over every human scheme. All of this comes to fullest expression in Christ, who identified with the poor, endured the Father's purpose through the cross, and now disciplines His people toward life.

context.literary:
Proverbs 19 stands in the middle of the long run of two line sentence proverbs that fill 10:1 to 22:16. It has no speeches and no plot, and its order is made by echo rather than argument. The poor man of verse 1 comes back in verses 4, 7 and 17. The false witness of verse 5 returns in verse 9 almost word for word, with the verdict hardened from 'will not escape' to 'will perish', and the same witness, now called corrupt, closes the chapter in verse 28. Those returns work as a frame, and between them the chapter moves back and forth between the social world of money, friends, kings and households, and the moral world of discipline, counsel and instruction, turning the first into a test of the second.

Two 'better than' sayings stand near the edges. Verse 1 prefers a poor man of integrity to a perverse fool, and verse 22 ends with 'better to be poor than a liar'. Between them the reader is taught that the honest poor are not the problem; the rich and the clever who lie are.

The centre holds a quiet pairing. Verses 20 and 21 turn on one Hebrew word, etsah. In verse 20 it is the counsel a pupil should hear; in verse 21 it is the purpose of the LORD that will stand. The arrangement suggests that learning to take advice is rehearsal, in small, for the submission the LORD's purpose asks in large. Verse 27 is the only place in the chapter where the teacher says 'my son', and the classroom voice of Proverbs 1 to 9 briefly surfaces inside the collection.
context.historical:
Tradition remembered Solomon as a prodigious maker of proverbs, 1 Kings 4:32, and his name stands over this collection at 10:1. The world the sayings assume is a village and court economy in which almost everything ran on relationship. Land was held by families, and verse 14 reminds us that 'houses and wealth are inherited from fathers'. A household's standing depended on brothers, neighbours and patrons. So when verse 7 says that all the brothers of a poor man hate him, it names a real fracture, because kin were meant to be the safety net. The law told them so. A countryman who became destitute was to be helped 'so that he can continue to live among you', Leviticus 25:35, and the poor were not to be charged interest, Exodus 22:25. Proverbs 19 does not deny that duty. It records how often it was ignored.

The court is also close at hand. The prince who is courted in verse 6 and the king whose rage and favour are weather in verse 12 belong to a world where access was bought with presents. The 'gift giver' of verse 6 is literally a man of gifts, mattan, the same word as in 18:16, 'A man's gift opens doors for him'. Such gifts were not always crooked, but they blurred easily into bribery, as 17:8 admits.

Verse 24, the slacker who buries his hand in the dish, repeats 26:15 almost exactly. That is a reminder that Israel's sages collected and reused sayings freely, and that a proverb was valued for being known, not for being new.
context.canonical:
Several of these sayings are the first form of teaching the rest of Scripture develops. Verse 17 stands on the law's command to open the hand to a poor brother and not to harden the heart, Deuteronomy 15:7 to 11, a passage that warns the poor man 'will cry out to the LORD against you' if he is refused. The psalmist makes the same promise, 'Blessed is the one who cares for the poor; the LORD will deliver him in the day of trouble', Psalm 41:1, and Proverbs 14:31 reads the matter as honour or contempt paid to the poor man's Maker. Jesus carries it to its sharpest form in Matthew 25:35 to 40, and Luke 6:35 asks His disciples to lend 'expecting nothing in return'.

Verse 18 on discipline is gathered up in Proverbs 3:11 to 12, 'the LORD disciplines the one He loves, as does a father the son in whom he delights', which Hebrews 12:5 to 6 quotes to explain suffering as sonship. Verse 21 belongs with Psalm 33:10 to 11, where the LORD frustrates the plans of the nations but His counsel stands forever, and with Isaiah 46:10, 'My purpose will stand'. Joseph says it of his brothers, Genesis 50:20, and the apostles say it of the cross, Acts 4:27 to 28. Verse 11 is the seed of James 1:19 to 20 on slowness to anger, and verse 1 returns almost word for word in Proverbs 28:6.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The sage wants the hearer to stop measuring a life by the measure the crowd uses. Wealth keeps failing as a test in this chapter. It gathers friends who vanish in need, buys a favour that lasts only as long as the gift, and cannot purchase a prudent wife, a patient temper or a teachable heart. Against it the teacher sets what cannot be inherited or bought: integrity, patience, instruction and the fear of the LORD.

He also wants the young listener to read the world soberly, without becoming hard. Verses 4 to 7 are not cynicism. They warn against building security on what only looks like loyalty, and they quietly ask the hearer not to be the friend who disappears when someone is poor. The same chapter that says the poor are deserted tells the reader, in verse 17, to be the one who does not desert.

Finally, he wants the plans of the heart held loosely. A student who has absorbed so many practical sayings could conclude that wisdom makes life controllable. Verse 21 corrects that. Wisdom works with the grain of what the LORD is doing; it never sits above it.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Three kinds of statement sit side by side. Some are plain commands, such as discipline your son, listen to counsel, and accept discipline, verses 18 and 20. Some are sober descriptions of how money bends social life, verses 4, 6 and 7, and these are not endorsements. To say that everyone is a friend of the gift giver is to expose the pattern so the reader refuses to join it. And some are promises of a general shape, such as verse 23, that the fear of the LORD leads to life.

The practical rule is to ask what the verse does with the situation it names. Verse 7 describes abandonment and then the chapter commands the opposite in verse 17. Verse 17 itself is a promise that God repays, but it is not a contract that guarantees a particular return in this life, and it does not turn charity into an investment strategy. Giving to the poor in order to be repaid would empty it of the kindness it names. Verse 15 and verse 24 on laziness are likewise observations about how idleness ends, and they are not a licence to treat every poor person as lazy, which verses 1 and 22 forbid.

debates.question: What does 'do not be party to his death' in verse 18 ask of a parent?

views.label: Do not stop correcting even when the child cries
views.case: The older English reading, 'let not thy soul spare for his crying', takes the verse to mean that a parent must not be moved by tears to withhold discipline. The urgency matches Proverbs 13:24 and 23:13 to 14, which treat discipline as a rescue from ruin.

views.label: Do not let your anger carry correction toward ruin
views.case: The BSB reading takes the closing phrase as a warning against destroying the child by excess or neglect. The next verse concerns a man of great anger, and Ephesians 6:4 later forbids fathers to provoke their children to wrath, which fits a caution against discipline driven by temper.

views.label: Do not be complicit in a child's self destruction by doing nothing
views.case: The verse says to discipline 'while there is hope', so the death in view may be the end of a life left uncorrected. Parental passivity, not cruelty, is the danger named.

debates.bearing: All three readings leave the main point standing: correction is a form of hope and it has a window. Read with Hebrews 12:10 to 11 and Ephesians 6:4, it calls for timely, loving discipline that aims at life. It cannot be used to excuse harshness, which the rest of Scripture rules out.

debates.question: Does verse 17 promise that generosity to the poor will be repaid with material blessing?

views.label: Yes, God returns it in kind, often in this life
views.case: The verb 'repay' and the commercial picture of a loan suggest a real return. Proverbs 11:25 and 28:27 say the generous prosper and the one who gives to the poor will not want, and Luke 6:38 speaks of a measure 'pressed down and running over'.

views.label: God repays surely, but on His terms and often beyond this life
views.case: Jesus ties the reward to the age to come, Luke 14:12 to 14, and Luke 6:35 says to lend 'expecting nothing in return'. The loan is secure because the Borrower is God, not because the return is predictable.

debates.bearing: Both views honour the certainty of the repayment. The second guards against two errors: using the verse as a formula for wealth, and thinking that an unrewarded gift was wasted. The one who lends to the LORD has the best debtor there is, who settles in His own coin and His own time.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 2 contains a word worth slowing down for. 'He who hurries his footsteps misses the mark' uses the verb chata. It is the ordinary Hebrew verb for sin, but in its older sense of missing a target. The sage is not calling haste sinful in itself. He is saying that enthusiasm without knowledge is like a man who draws the bow with energy and has not looked at what he is aiming at. Sin, in Hebrew, begins as a failure of aim.

Verse 17 is rich in small words. The lender is a malveh, and the poor man's helper is called one who shows chonen, a participle from the root of grace and favour. The one who is gracious to the poor is therefore doing something that sounds like the LORD's own work, since the same root marks the LORD as gracious, Exodus 34:6. The closing verb 'repay' is a form of shalam, the root that gives us shalom, wholeness and full settlement. A debt paid shalam is made whole. The line then ends with gemul, the word for what a person has dealt out, so the sentence promises that the LORD will return to the giver his own dealing, completed.

Verses 20 and 21 share etsah, 'counsel' in the first and 'purpose' in the second, and the plural 'plans' of verse 21 uses a word for what the heart devises, machashavot, found also in Proverbs 16:3. The contrast is one of scale: many devisings, one etsah. Psalm 33:10 to 11 sets the same two words against each other, the plans of the nations and the counsel of the LORD that stands.

Verse 6 names the man of gifts with the word mattan, 'a present'. Together with 18:16 and 21:14 it shows the proverb tradition tracking gifts as the currency of favour, with the sharper word shochad, 'bribe', used when the gift turns crooked, 17:8.

Two verses are notoriously difficult. The last clause of verse 7, 'they are nowhere to be found', is obscure in Hebrew and translations vary. Verse 22 is similarly hard. The BSB renders it 'The desire of a man is loving devotion', taking chesed in a good sense, while other translations take it as what makes a man desirable, his kindness or loyalty. Either way, the verse ends firmly: a poor man is better than a liar.

typology.type: The poor man deserted by friends and kin, verse 7
typology.fulfillment: The poor man pleads and finds no one. In the garden and at the trial the pattern comes to its sharpest instance: 'everyone deserted Him and fled', Mark 14:50, and the Man who had once healed and fed them stood alone. The correspondence is real, and it reaches further in Christ, who 'though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor', 2 Corinthians 8:9. It falls short in one place that matters. The proverb's poor man is helpless and stays abandoned. Christ chose the poverty, and when He rose He came back through locked doors to the same friends with 'Peace be with you', John 20:19.

typology.type: The loan to the LORD, verse 17
typology.fulfillment: The proverb pictures God as the debtor who takes on what is lent to the poor. Jesus makes that identification literal, 'whatever you did for one of the least of these brothers of Mine, you did for Me', Matthew 25:40, and He preaches good news 'to the poor', Luke 4:18. The type is fulfilled and turned over: Christ is not only the poor man who receives but the Lender who cancelled a debt no one could pay, 'having canceled the debt ascribed to us', Colossians 2:14. It still falls short as a type of payment. The proverb has God repaying the giver, while the gospel has God paying the whole debt Himself.

A correction offered in time, before the window closes. Hebrews 12:5 to 11 reads this proverb, and its parent text in Proverbs 3:11 to 12, as God's treatment of every child He receives. The Son of God belongs inside the pattern, since 'although He was a Son, He learned obedience from what He suffered', Hebrews 5:8. The escalation is that His suffering was not correction for any fault, but the way the Father brought many sons to glory. The type fails when pressed too hard: the human father may be harsh or wrong, while the heavenly Father's discipline is always 'for our good, so that we may share in His holiness', Hebrews 12:10.

study.christ:
This chapter never names the Messiah, so the road to Christ runs through pattern and theme, and each link needs to be tied to a New Testament text.

The first link is the poor man. Verses 4 to 7 describe the experience of being deserted, and they are an uncomfortable fit for the gospel accounts of Jesus' last hours. He was handed over by one friend, denied by another, and 'everyone deserted Him and fled', Mark 14:50. He was also falsely accused. 'The chief priests and the whole Sanhedrin were seeking false testimony against Jesus', Matthew 26:59, and the false witnesses of verses 5, 9 and 28 are there in the story. Proverbs says such a witness 'will not go unpunished', and the story of the false testimony at His trial is told so that the reader sees how far lies can travel and who in the end bears them.

The second link is verse 17. Christ is the poor man whose cause is God's own, and He is also the one who makes a gift to the poor a gift to Himself. 'Though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor, so that you through His poverty might become rich', 2 Corinthians 8:9. The loan to the LORD is secured by a Borrower who entered poverty on purpose.

The third link is verse 21. At Gethsemane Jesus prays, 'Not My will, but Yours be done', Luke 22:42, and the apostles later say the powers that killed Him 'carried out what Your hand and will had decided beforehand', Acts 4:28. Many plans, one purpose. The cross shows both at full strength, wicked designs and holy design, without the second being made complicit in the first.

Last, verse 11 prizes the virtue of overlooking an offence. At the cross He says, 'Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing', Luke 23:34. This is wisdom in its fullest form, and it is the pattern His people are called to follow when they are wronged.
study.god:
The chapter's picture of God holds three things together that are easy to separate.

First, He is sovereign and still near. Verse 21 says that among the many plans in the human heart the purpose of the LORD will prevail, and verse 14 says that a prudent wife, the best of domestic gifts, is from the LORD. These sit in the same chapter as the plain statement in verse 3 that a man's own folly subverts his way, and yet he rages at the LORD. The sage does not resolve this; he shows both. A person ruins his life by his own hand and blames God for it, which is exactly the move Adam makes in Genesis 3:12, 'The woman whom You gave me'. God's sovereignty is never offered as an excuse in this book. It is offered as a refuge.

Second, He is a Father who disciplines in hope. Verse 18 sets discipline inside a home, and the New Testament lets us hear God's own voice there, Hebrews 12:5 to 6. The God of the chapter is not indifferent to a child's drift. He treats it as urgent and as worth the pain of correction.

Third, He is a debtor who stands behind the poor. Verse 17 does not say that God is pleased by kindness to the poor. It says that the kindness is a loan to Him and that He will repay. A God who identifies His own name with the destitute is not one who can be thought of as a distant patron of the powerful. The commercial words fit a Lord who treats a cup of water to the least as business with Him.

For worship this means thanks for gifts we did not earn, such as a faithful spouse or a household, honest repentance when we blame Him for what we did ourselves, and a humble willingness to say with the sage that our best plans are worth holding only if the LORD's purpose is in them. Verse 23 holds out the reward of that humility: the fear of the LORD leads to life, and a person can rest content.

crossReferences.note: Almost the same saying as verse 1, with a rich man whose ways are perverse in place of a fool whose lips are perverse. The repetition shows the sages treated this ranking of integrity above income as settled, and the change of subject shows the same charge can be laid against the powerful and the foolish alike.

The same observation as verse 4 and verse 7, in a different form: the poor man is hated even by his neighbour, while many love the rich. Placed side by side the two proverbs read as a pattern the sages kept seeing, not a single mood.

The law behind verse 17. Israel is told to open the hand and loan freely to a poor brother, and not to count how near the year of release is. The warning that he may cry out to the LORD against the one who refuses is the dark side of the same truth: the poor have a Defender.

Jesus gives the loan of verse 17 a face. The righteous fed, clothed and visited the least of His brothers without knowing they served the King. The proverb says the LORD repays the lender. Jesus says the kindness was done to Him.

Jesus tells His disciples to lend 'expecting nothing in return', and promises a great reward and sonship of the Most High. It guards verse 17 from being read as a business deal and shows the repayment is God's gift, not the giver's claim.

Quotes Proverbs 3:11 to 12 and carries verse 18 to its depth. Discipline is the sign of sonship, painful for the moment, and it yields 'a harvest of righteousness and peace'. The earthly father who disciplines while there is hope is a picture of the Father who never stops.

The psalm sets the plans of the nations against the counsel of the LORD that stands forever, using the same contrast as verse 21. Taken together they show it was a settled conviction of Israel's worship as well as its wisdom.

The believers pray about the cross in the language of verse 21: Herod, Pilate, the nations and Israel conspired, yet they carried out what God's hand and will had decided beforehand. It is the sharpest test of the proverb, and the church's answer is worship.

Joseph tells his brothers that what they meant for evil God meant for good. Here is verse 21 lived out in a family: their plan and God's purpose were both real, and only one of them determined how the story ended.

Quick to listen, slow to speak and slow to anger, because 'man's anger does not bring about the righteousness that God desires'. It is the New Testament form of verse 11, where insight gives patience and overlooking an offence is counted a virtue.

Whoever finds a wife finds a good thing and obtains favour from the LORD. It stands beside verse 14, where a prudent wife is from the LORD, and together they treat marriage as a gift received more than a prize won.

study.oneStory:
Proverbs 19 sits in the story at the point where the question of Eden has become a daily one: whom will we trust to tell us what is good? In Genesis 3 the man and the woman reached for what looked desirable and found themselves naked, alone and blaming each other, and the man blamed God Himself, 'the woman whom You gave me'. Verse 3 is that scene in one line: a man's folly subverts his way, and then his heart rages against the LORD. The chapter's observations about money, friends and favour describe life outside the garden, where goods are scarce, trust is fragile and the strong take advantage of the weak.

Against that, the chapter keeps a record of what God has not abandoned. Israel's law made the poor the LORD's special charge, and the sages repeat it, so that to lend to the poor is to lend to Him. The LORD's purpose, verse 21, is the thread through the tangle. Genesis follows it through Joseph, Exodus through Pharaoh, and the prophets through exile and return, and in each case human plans collide with it and give way.

The story arrives at Christ, who enters the world of verses 4 to 7 on purpose, becoming poor, deserted and falsely accused, and in doing so He pays the debt the proverbs could only describe. His Father disciplines Him toward obedience and exalts Him. In His death the many plans of the human heart and the one purpose of the LORD meet, and the purpose stands.

The end of the story answers the chapter's anxieties directly. In the new creation the poor 'will never again hunger', Revelation 7:16, and the Lamb is their shepherd, who wipes away every tear. Nobody there is deserted, nobody needs to buy a friend, and the fear of the LORD, which verse 23 says leads to life, has become the delight of a people who live with Him, Revelation 21:3 to 4.

quiz.q: According to verse 1, what is better than a fool with perverse lips?

options.text: A poor man who walks with integrity.
options.note: Integrity outweighs both wealth and eloquence when character is corrupt.

options.text: A rich man with perverse lips.
options.note: This is the very thing the verse ranks below integrity.

options.text: A wealthy man of few words.
options.note: Wealth is not the point of comparison in this verse; integrity versus folly is.

options.text: A poor man who is also foolish.
options.note: The verse specifically praises poverty paired with integrity, not with foolishness.

quiz.q: What does verse 17 say about kindness to the poor?

options.text: It is a loan to the LORD, and He will repay the lender.
options.note: Mercy to the poor is treated as a debt God Himself takes on and repays.

options.text: It is wasted generosity with no lasting effect.
options.note: The verse promises repayment from the LORD, not futility.

options.text: It obligates the poor person to repay the giver directly.
options.note: The repayment comes from the LORD, not from the poor person helped.

options.text: It is commendable but carries no promise attached.
options.note: The verse explicitly attaches a promise, that the LORD will repay.

quiz.q: What does verse 21 declare about human plans and the LORD's purpose?

options.text: Many plans are in a man's heart, but the purpose of the LORD will prevail.
options.note: Human planning is real but subordinate to God's overruling purpose.

options.text: Human plans always fail completely.
options.note: The verse contrasts plans with the LORD's prevailing purpose, not declaring all plans failures outright.

options.text: The LORD has no purpose of His own, only reacting to human plans.
options.note: This is the opposite; the LORD's purpose is what finally prevails.

options.text: Human plans and the LORD's purpose are always identical.
options.note: The verse implies real tension between the two, resolved by the LORD's purpose prevailing, not by automatic identity.

quiz.q: What does verse 18 urge concerning a son?

options.text: Discipline him while there is hope, and do not be party to his death.
options.note: Timely, hope-filled correction is urged with real urgency.

options.text: Wait until adulthood before offering any correction.
options.note: The verse's urgency, 'while there is hope,' argues against delay.

options.text: Discipline is optional if the son seems naturally good.
options.note: The verse gives no such exception; the call to discipline is general.

options.text: Discipline should be applied only occasionally.
options.note: The verse's urgency suggests sustained, timely correction, not mere occasional action.

quiz.q: What does verse 23 say the fear of the LORD leads to?

options.text: Life, and rest without harm.
options.note: Reverent fear of God is tied to genuine security and life.

options.text: Constant anxiety and unrest.
options.note: This is the opposite of the rest the verse promises.

options.text: Wealth and social status.
options.note: The verse's promise is life and rest, not material wealth or status.

options.text: A general sense of caution, without real security.
options.note: The verse promises more than caution; it promises life and rest from harm.

questions: Verse 1 prizes integrity over cleverness or wealth. Where are you tempted to cut corners on character to get ahead?
Wealth attracts many friends, but poverty scatters even family, verses 4 and 7. Has your own capacity for friendship been shaped more by what people can offer you than by love?
Kindness to the poor is called a loan to the LORD, verse 17. What would change in your giving if you truly believed God Himself was the one repaying it?
Many plans fill the human heart, but the LORD's purpose prevails, verse 21. What plan are you gripping tightly that you need to hold with an open hand before God?
Verse 20 calls us to listen to counsel and accept discipline for a lifetime of wisdom. Whose correction have you been resisting that you need to receive humbly this week?

translationNotes.note: 'Luxury is unseemly for a fool' pictures social order upended, a related image to a slave ruling over princes, both describing things that violate a fitting, expected order.
'Do not be party to his death' can also be rendered 'do not set your heart on his destruction,' meaning withholding correction is a kind of complicity in the child's ruin.
The image of a slacker burying his hand in the dish yet failing to bring it to his mouth repeats at 26:15, a vivid caricature of paralyzing laziness.

meta.notes: BSB text fetched via the Makor scripture toolkit for Proverbs 19.
